43.title: Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38)
43.hook: two old people who waited their whole lives recognize the baby in the temple
43.howItsDone: Many churches keep the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, often called Candlemas, when candles are blessed. Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, is sung or said at the close of the day in Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox prayer.

screen: `DAY FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherds: the night shift heard the news first, and Mary kept it all. Your line was ponder it in your heart. What moment did you keep? Today the days of Mary and Nazareth come to a close. Day forty-three.
screen: `PONDER IT IN YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Forty days after a birth, the law of Moses asked a mother to come to the temple, and a firstborn son was presented to God. So Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to Jerusalem. They bring the offering the law allowed for families who couldn't afford a lamb: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The temple courts are loud. Pilgrims, priests, animals, coins changing hands. Nobody is watching a young couple from Galilee with a baby and two birds. Nobody except two people. Two very old people, who have been waiting for a very long time, and who know what they're looking at. Today, Simeon and Anna.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OLD.` → `TWO BIRDS, NOT A LAMB.` → `TWO OLD PEOPLE, WAITING.`

segments.voice: Luke introduces Simeon in the King James Bible like this: "the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." Waiting for the comfort of his people. Luke says the Spirit had shown him he would not die before he saw the one God promised. So that day he's led into the temple, and he takes the baby in his arms, and he says: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." He calls the child a light for the nations and the glory of Israel. In Latin those first words are Nunc dimittis, now you let go, and Simeon's song has been sung at the end of the day for well over a thousand years: at evening prayer by Anglicans, at night prayer by Catholics, at vespers by Orthodox Christians. Then he turns to Mary with a harder word: a sword will pierce her own soul too. And then Anna. A prophetess, Luke says, very old, married seven years and then a widow, "which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Luke gives a number, eighty-four, and nobody is sure whether it's her age or the years she'd been a widow. She comes up in that same hour, gives thanks, and starts telling everyone who is waiting too. Notice who recognizes the child here. Not the powerful. Two people who kept showing up. In the Bible, waiting isn't sitting still. It's coming back, day after day, looking.
screen: `JUST AND DEVOUT, WAITING.` · `NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART.` · `A SWORD FOR MARY'S SOUL.` · `ANNA, NIGHT AND DAY.` · then, large: `MINE EYES HAVE SEEN THY SALVATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of someone older than you who has waited a long time for something. A grandparent who waited for a letter. A neighbor who waited out an illness. Someone still waiting for a phone call from a child. Bring their face to mind. What did the waiting cost them? What did it teach them? Just sit with them for a while. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, honor them quietly in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Simeon and Anna. The old man who held the baby and said now I can go in peace, and the widow who never left the temple. The last faces in the story of Mary and Nazareth.
screen: `SIMEON AND ANNA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: waiting is not wasted. Today, honor one elder who has waited long: a call, a visit, a real question about their life. Tomorrow the road opens toward Galilee, and it starts with stargazers from the east. Day forty-three.

44.title: The magi (Matthew 2:1–12)
44.hook: stargazers from the east follow a light and kneel before a toddler
44.howItsDone: Western churches celebrate the magi at Epiphany on January 6, and in many countries children mark it with processions, sweets or chalked blessings over doorways. In Orthodox churches January 6 centers on the baptism of Jesus, and the magi are remembered at Christmas.

screen: `DAY FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon and Anna, two old people who knew the child when he came. Your line was waiting is not wasted. Who did you honor? Today a new stretch of the road begins, the road through Galilee. Day forty-four.
screen: `WAITING IS NOT WASTED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who stays up late looking at the sky. Not for a reason, exactly. Just because something up there keeps pulling at them. Now picture a small group of them, far to the east of Jerusalem, men who study the night sky for meaning. One night they see something they can't ignore. They pack up and travel, for weeks, maybe months, following it west. And when they finally reach the capital, they walk into a king's court and ask the most dangerous question in the room. In the King James Bible: "Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him." The king on the throne is Herod. Today, the magi.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO WATCHES THE SKY.` → `A STAR IN THE EAST.` → `WHERE IS HE THAT IS BORN KING?`

segments.voice: Matthew calls them magoi, and he never says how many there were. Three is a guess, made later, from the three gifts. He never calls them kings either; that came later too, from psalms about kings bringing gifts. And their names, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, come from legends written centuries after. What the word magoi meant was something like wise men or astrologers: learned stargazers, probably from Persia or Babylon, outsiders to Israel's faith. Herod is troubled, Matthew says, and all Jerusalem with him. His scholars look it up: the prophet Micah points to Bethlehem. Herod sends the visitors on, and asks them to come back and tell him where the child is, so that he can worship too. He doesn't mean it. They go, and the star goes before them, and when it stops, the King James says, "they rejoiced with exceeding great joy." Exceeding great joy. Matthew piles up the words. They find the child with Mary his mother, in a house now, not a stable, and they kneel. Then they open their treasures: "gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." Christians have read the gifts for centuries as gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh for a death to come. Then, warned in a dream, they go home another way. Here's what's striking: the first people in Matthew's Gospel to worship Jesus are foreigners, following the light they had, a star, not a scripture. Western churches remember them on Epiphany, January sixth, the day the light is shown to the nations.
screen: `NO NUMBER, NO CROWNS, NO NAMES.` · `STARGAZERS FROM THE EAST.` · `GOLD, FRANKINCENSE AND MYRRH.` · `HOME ANOTHER WAY.` · then, large: `THEY REJOICED WITH EXCEEDING GREAT JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Now ask: what has been pulling at my attention lately? Not a duty. A curiosity. A question you keep coming back to, a book you keep meaning to open, a person you'd like to know better, a place you keep wondering about. Don't judge whether it's important. The magi followed a light in the sky. Just find yours and look at it for a while. If you pray, you can ask where it leads. The bell holds the time.
The magi. Stargazers from the east, no number given, who followed a light and knelt before a child. Our word magic comes from the same root.
screen: `THE MAGI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: follow the star you have. Today, follow one small curiosity, just one step further than you normally would. Day forty-four.

45.title: The flight into Egypt (Matthew 2:13–23)
45.hook: the holy family become refugees, fleeing a king's violence by night
45.howItsDone: Many churches remember the flight into Egypt in the days after Christmas, along with the Holy Innocents, and many Christian charities point to this story in their work with refugees. Coptic Christians celebrate the Holy Family's arrival in Egypt each year and visit places tradition links to their journey.

screen: `DAY FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the magi: stargazers who followed a light and went home another way. Your line was follow the star you have. What curiosity did you follow? Day forty-five.
screen: `FOLLOW THE STAR YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Picture a family packing in the dark. No time to say goodbye. Whatever fits in their arms, and a child who doesn't understand why he's been woken up. They leave before sunrise, heading for a border, because staying means someone they love may be killed. That happens somewhere in the world tonight. In Matthew's Gospel it happens to Mary, Joseph and the child. The magi have gone home another way, and Herod, the king who asked where the child was, has worked out that he's been tricked. And Joseph has another dream. Today, the flight into Egypt.
screen: `PACKING IN THE DARK.` → `HEROD HAS BEEN TRICKED.` → `JOSEPH DREAMS AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The angel's words in the King James Bible are urgent: "Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him." And Joseph does it that same night. Notice Joseph again. He never speaks a single word in the Gospels. He just gets up and goes. Then comes the darkest scene in the Christmas story. Herod, furious, orders every boy of two and under in and around Bethlehem to be killed. Matthew is the only source for this; no other writer from the time mentions it, though Herod was known to be ruthless, even with his own sons. Matthew quotes the prophet Jeremiah: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." The story doesn't hurry past the grief. Churches still keep a day for these children, the Holy Innocents, in the days after Christmas. Egypt, the old land of slavery in the Exodus story, is now the place of safety. Matthew quotes another prophet, Hosea: "Out of Egypt have I called my son." Israel's story is being lived again in one child. Coptic Christians in Egypt still trace the places they say the family stayed, and they celebrate the family's arrival every year. Then Herod dies, and Joseph dreams again, and they come home, not to Bethlehem but to a small town in Galilee called Nazareth. So before he preached, before he healed, before anyone knew his name, Jesus was a child carried across a border by night.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one family that has had to leave home. Maybe you know them. Maybe you saw them in the news. Maybe it's your own family, a generation or two back. Picture them as clearly as you can: the packing, the road, the first night somewhere strange. Hold them there. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or for the family whose name you'll never know. If you don't pray, just keep them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
The flight into Egypt. A family running from a king's violence by night, and finding safety in the old land of slavery.

46.title: The boy in the temple (Luke 2:41–52)
46.hook: twelve-year-old Jesus goes missing for three days and is found asking questions
46.tomorrow: The wild man by the river
46.howItsDone: Many churches read this story in the Christmas season, and Catholics pray it as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the finding in the temple. Bible study groups and confirmation classes often begin from it, since it shows the young Jesus asking questions.

screen: `DAY FORTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flight into Egypt, a family running by night. Your line was he was a refugee first. Did you stop to picture one family? Day forty-six.
screen: `HE WAS A REFUGEE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Every parent knows the feeling. You turn around in a crowded store and your kid isn't there. Your stomach drops. Now stretch that feeling out to three days. Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem every year for Passover, Luke says, and this year Jesus is twelve. When the feast ends they start home, traveling with a big group of relatives and neighbors, and they assume he's somewhere in the crowd. A whole day's walk later they look for him, and he's gone. They turn around. Three days of searching a packed city. Today, the boy in the temple.
screen: `WHERE'S THE KID?` → `A WHOLE DAY'S WALK.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: They find him in the temple courts, and look at what he's doing. In the King James Bible: "sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the rabbis and scholars of the law. He isn't lecturing them. He's listening, and asking. Luke says everyone who heard him was astonished at his understanding and his answers. Then Mary speaks, and every parent will recognize it: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." And the boy's answer is the first thing Jesus ever says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Here's a small puzzle. The Greek is short and can be read two ways: about my Father's business, or in my Father's house. Translators still choose between them. Either way, the first words he speaks point to God as his Father. And his parents, Luke says plainly, didn't understand. He goes home with them and is obedient to them, and Mary, again, keeps all these sayings in her heart. This is the only story in the four Gospels from the years between his infancy and his adult life. Eighteen years or so of silence, and the one scene we're given is a boy asking questions in the house of God. Then one line for everything after: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." He grew. Even he grew, a little at a time.
screen: `FOUND AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `HEARING THEM, AND ASKING THEM.` · `MY FATHER'S BUSINESS, OR HOUSE?` · `THE ONLY STORY FROM THOSE YEARS.` · then, large: `JESUS INCREASED IN WISDOM AND STATURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself get quiet. Now look for a question you've been carrying. About God, about your life, about something you were taught that never quite made sense. A real one, not a polite one. Some people hide their questions because they think faith means having answers. The boy in this story sits in the temple asking. So find yours. Say it to yourself plainly, in one sentence. If you pray, you can bring it to God just as it is. The bell holds the time.
The boy in the temple. Twelve years old, missing for three days, found listening and asking questions among the teachers.

47.title: The wild man by the river (Mark 1:4–8)
47.word: The wild man by the river
47.hook: John the Baptist in camel hair calls people to turn around
47.howItsDone: Many Christians remember John the Baptist during Advent, the weeks before Christmas, when his call to prepare the way is read in church. His birth is celebrated on June 24, and in many traditions repentance is practiced through confession, private or shared, and a fresh start.

screen: `DAY FORTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy in the temple, found asking questions. Your line was questions belong in the temple. What did you finally ask? Now the story jumps about eighteen years. Day forty-seven.
screen: `QUESTIONS BELONG IN THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Imagine a man living outside town, in the wild. He wears rough clothes woven from camel hair, with a leather belt. He eats what he can find: locusts and wild honey. No house, no title, no invitation. And crowds walk out of the city to hear him. Mark's Gospel doesn't open with a manger. It opens here, in the desert by the Jordan River, with this man shouting. His name is John, and people will call him John the Baptist. Mark says the whole region of Judea went out to him, and people from Jerusalem too. What was he saying that was worth the walk? Today, the wild man by the river.
screen: `CAMEL HAIR AND A LEATHER BELT.` → `LOCUSTS AND WILD HONEY.` → `CROWDS WALK OUT TO HEAR HIM.`

segments.voice: Mark begins with a line from the prophet Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." Then: "John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins." Repentance is a heavy church word. Here's what's inside it. The Greek is metanoia: meta, change, and noia, from the word for mind. A change of mind. The Hebrew prophets used a simpler word, shuv: turn around, go back. So when John preaches repentance, the picture isn't mainly groveling. It's a person walking the wrong way who stops, turns, and heads home. Then he washes them in the river. Water had long been used in Jewish life for washing and becoming clean, and John makes it a sign of a fresh start. And his clothes are a message too: the Bible describes the prophet Elijah the same way, hairy, with a leather belt. People would have noticed. But the most surprising thing is what John says about himself: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose." Untying sandals was a servant's job. John has crowds, fame, a following, and he spends it all pointing past himself. I baptize you with water, he says. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. John's whole job is to get people turned around and facing the right way, so they'll recognize the one who's coming. A Jewish historian of the time, Josephus, remembered him too, as a good man who called people to live justly.
screen: `A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `METANOIA: A CHANGE OF MIND.` · `SHUV: TURN AROUND, GO BACK.` · `NOT WORTHY TO UNTIE HIS SANDALS.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle in, and breathe slowly. Now think about direction, not guilt. Is there one small thing you keep walking toward that takes you somewhere you don't want to go? A habit, a tone of voice with someone, a scroll at midnight, a grudge. Something small enough to name. Just name it, quietly. Then picture yourself stopping, and turning around. Not a big dramatic scene. Just a turn. If you pray, you can ask for help turning. The bell holds the time.
The wild man by the river. John the Baptist, in camel hair, calling crowds to turn around, and pointing past himself to someone greater.

segments.voice: Your line: turn around. start again. Today, when you catch yourself heading toward the thing you named, just turn. As many times as it takes. Day forty-seven.

48.title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
48.hook: Jesus goes under the Jordan, and a voice says: this is my beloved son
48.howItsDone: Nearly all Christians are baptized with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as infants in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches, and as believers in Baptist and many other churches. Many churches keep the Baptism of the Lord in January, and Orthodox Christians bless water at Theophany.

screen: `DAY FORTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wild man by the river, calling crowds to change their minds. Your line was turn around. start again. Did you turn? Today someone new walks down to John's river. Day forty-eight.
screen: `TURN AROUND. START AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Think about the first time someone really told you they loved you. Not because you'd earned it. Not because you'd done something impressive. Just because. Most of us spend a lot of life trying to earn that sentence. Now go back to the Jordan River. John is baptizing crowds, people turning around and starting again. And one day a man from Nazareth, about thirty years old, joins the line. He hasn't preached a sermon. He hasn't healed anyone. As far as anyone knows, he's a builder from a small town in Galilee. And John looks at him and stops. Today's word: baptism.
screen: `LOVED, JUST BECAUSE.` → `A MAN FROM NAZARETH JOINS THE LINE.` → `JOHN STOPS.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, to plunge, to immerse. It's an ordinary word. You could baptize a cloth in dye. John tries to refuse, in the King James Bible: "I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?" Jesus answers: "Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness." Suffer here means allow. Let it happen. So he goes down into the water, like everyone else in the line. Christians have wondered at that for two thousand years: why would he stand with people turning from their wrongs? Many answer that he chose to stand exactly where they stood. Then he comes up out of the water, and Matthew says "the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him." And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at the timing. He hasn't done anything yet. No miracles, no teaching, no followers. The voice calls him beloved first, and the work comes after. Christians see here the Father's voice, the Son in the water, and the Spirit like a dove, all in one scene, and many churches keep this day as the feast of the Baptism of the Lord. Orthodox Christians call it Theophany, God shown, and bless water. And baptism itself became the door into the church, though churches do it differently. Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and many others baptize babies. Baptists and many other churches baptize those old enough to profess faith. Some pour, some sprinkle, some go all the way under. Nearly all use water and the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
screen: `BAPTIZO: TO DIP, TO PLUNGE.` · `HE STANDS IN LINE WITH EVERYONE.` · `A DOVE AND A VOICE.` · `ONE WATER, MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you can, go to a sink. Turn on the water, let it run warm, and hold your hands under it. Slowly. Feel it run over your fingers and your palms. If you can't get to water, just rest your hands open in your lap and imagine it. While it runs, notice that you haven't done anything to earn this moment. You're just here. If you pray, you can hear the word beloved as spoken to you. If not, just let the water be water. The bell holds the time.
Baptism. From the Greek for dip or plunge. Washing with water as a door into a new life, and the scene where Jesus is called beloved before he does a thing.

49.title: Forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11)
49.hook: hungry and alone, he's offered bread, spectacle and power, and says no three times
49.howItsDone: Many churches keep Lent, the forty days before Easter, in memory of these forty days, with fasting, prayer and giving; the temptation story is often read on the first Sunday of Lent. Practices range from giving up a food or habit to fasting on set days.

screen: `DAY FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism: the voice that called him beloved before he'd done a thing. Your line was beloved, before anything else. Today that word gets tested. And it's the end of week seven. Day forty-nine.
screen: `BELOVED, BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: You know what it's like to be really hungry. Not snack hungry. Skipped-two-meals hungry, where everything gets louder and your judgment gets worse. Now multiply it. Right after the voice at the river, Matthew says, the Spirit leads Jesus up into the wilderness, the dry, empty hills near the Jordan. He fasts forty days and forty nights. And then, the text says, with a kind of dry understatement, he was hungry. That's when the tempter comes. Not at the start, when he's strong. At the end, when he's weakest. Today, forty days in the wilderness.
screen: `REALLY HUNGRY.` → `FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS.` → `THE TEMPTER COMES AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Listen to the first words, in the King James Bible: "If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread." If. The voice at the river just said, this is my beloved Son. The first temptation goes straight for that: prove it. The answer: "It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God." Then the tempter takes him to the highest point of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. A spectacle. Make them believe. And Jesus answers: "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Then a high mountain, and all the kingdoms of the world, offered in exchange for one act of worship. Power, the fast way. "Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve." Three offers: bread, spectacle, power. Three refusals. And here's the detail a careful reader notices. All three answers come from one book, Deuteronomy, from the chapters where Moses remembers Israel's forty years in the wilderness, when they were hungry and tested too. Forty years for a people, forty days for one man. He answers with the words his people learned in the desert. And that forty is why many churches keep Lent, forty days before Easter, fasting a little and saying no to something. This week began in the temple with Simeon and Anna. Then the magi, a family fleeing to Egypt, a boy asking questions, a wild man by the river, the baptism, and now the desert. Beloved first. Then tested.
screen: `IF THOU BE THE SON OF GOD.` · `BREAD, SPECTACLE, POWER.` · `THREE ANSWERS FROM DEUTERONOMY.` · `FORTY YEARS, FORTY DAYS.` · then, large: `NOT BY BREAD ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your body settle. Think of one small temptation that tends to find you on an ordinary day. The extra hour on the phone. The sharp reply. The thing you buy to feel better. The shortcut. Not the biggest one, just one you'll meet today. Picture the moment it usually arrives, when you're tired or hungry or bored. Now picture yourself saying no to it, once, calmly. If you pray, you can ask for strength for that moment. The bell holds the time.
Forty days in the wilderness. Hunger, three offers, three refusals. This week's words: Simeon and Anna, the magi, the flight into Egypt, the boy in the temple, the wild man by the river, baptism.
